Numerous heavy showers and isolated thunderstorms moved across Guam 
through much of the day today. Some 2 to 4 inches of rain were 
reported by rain gauges and reports from observers. The afternoon 
rainfall total at WFO Guam was 2.35 inches. Additional showers and 
thunderstorms are expected tonight, which could lead to flooding 
concerns, especially across southern Guam. Shower coverage looks to 
decrease Friday through Sunday as the southern end of the monsoon 
decreases in shower activity. As the pattern dries out, breezy 
conditions will return this weekend. 

Uncertainty remains high in the evolution of the broader pattern 
next week as several disturbances look to interact with the monsoon 
trough. Model guidance is in a relatively good agreement that there 
will be a few disturbances racing eastward north of the CNMI next 
week, however models vary greatly on both location and intensity. 
Some guidance bring a couple of disturbances further south into the 
Far Northern Marianas Islands. This scenario shifts the monsoon 
surge south over the CNMI and Guam, leading to higher impacts from 
wind and rain next week. Other guidance shows the disturbances 
either moving further north, or becoming more organized. This 
scenario shifts the strongest winds and rain north of CNMI and Guam. 
Overall, direct impacts from these disturbances are not expected for 
the CNMI and Guam, but the influence on the monsoon surge will 
greatly depend on where the disturbances track and how strong they 
become. If trends shift the monsoon surge southward next week, then 
hydrological products may be needed for the Marianas next week.

Marine...
Combined seas remain between 8 and 11 feet and are expected to 
remain within that range through tonight. A slight decrease in seas 
is expected Friday before another increase this weekend. The Small 
Craft Advisory is now in effect until Monday morning. Pounding surf 
of 10 to 12 feet will continue through the weekend along west and 
north facing reefs. The High Surf Advisory and High Risk of Rip 
Currents was extended until Monday afternoon. These marine hazards 
could continue into next week as the monsoon pattern intensifies over
the region.

Tropical Systems...
Invest 96W is located along the edge of Guam's AOR (Area of
Responsibility), centered near 26N164E. The Joint Typhoon Warning
Center (JTWC) rates 96W as "medium" for development, meaning it will
likely develop into a significant tropical cyclone, but not within
the next 24 hours. ASCAT winds from this morning depict a much 
healthier low-level circulation compared to yesterday evening, but 
still broad and asymmetrical. 25 to 35 knot winds are seen throughout
96W's western to northeastern flanks, extending outward 400 miles 
north of the center, with some smaller areas exceeding 40 knots. Wind
speeds are lower south of the disturbance, around 10 to 20 knots 
within the southeastern to southwestern flanks. Satellite imagery
shows a broad area of deep, flaring convection wrapping into the
center with the tail extending far to the south near Wake Island. 
Model guidance keeps 96W along a generally northwest track as it 
continues to exit the region.

For more information on Invest 96W, please refer to bulletins from
the Joint Typhoon Warning Center under WMO Header ABPQ10 PGTW.

Eastern Micronesia...
Not much has changed as the monsoon trough remains north of the
region, maintaining a west to southwest flow. The best convergence
and moisture is north of the region as it wraps into Invest 96W north
of Wake Island, with just light to gentle winds prevalent across the
region. As such, only isolated showers and perhaps a thunderstorm can
be expected through next week.

As for marine conditions, altimetry showed sea heights of 7 to 8 feet
near Pohnpei, with lower heights south and east. Both Wave Watch III
and GFS Global Wave show surf will remain low enough to precluding
any headline necessity, as both models indicate 4 to 5 foot swell at
13 seconds, well short of criteria for any High Surf Advisory. Seas
look to drop a foot or so through the weekend, with light to gentle
winds prevailing.

Western Micronesia...
A drier pattern persists well south of the monsoon surge. A band of 
deep convection has been focused over Guam, oriented from northwest 
to southeast, and swaths of upper-level cloud debris are streaming
southward across the outer islands of Yap and over northern Chuuk 
State. Outflow boundaries associated with prior convection are
sweeping just north of Weno and could produce brief moderate showers 
or even a thunderstorm or two this evening over its coastal waters.
Over Palau and Yap, partly cloudy skies prevail, with light, isolated
shower bands and roughly 10 to 20 knot winds across the region. A 
similar pattern will prevail through the weekend and much of the 
coming week, as the monsoon trough, and associated monsoon surge, 
remain well north of the region.
